population.note: FICTIONAL. Base: ~272M adults. Current users: 13.7% ≈ 37.3M. Ever-used: 25.6% ≈ 69.6M. Used and off now: 11.9% ≈ 32.4M. Cycling arithmetic: about 7.4 pts of current users are on a second or later course, and about 4.4 pts of the off-now group restarted at least once and stopped again, so (7.4+4.4)/25.6 ≈ 46% cycled, up from 42%. That fits one-year persistence slipping from ~35% to ~32% as gated employer coverage ends, with restarts still running ~35–45% a year through $199 cash and imports. Ever-use rose only 1.6 pts (≈4.4M first-time users) because state in-person and age rules slowed new telehealth starts. Age check: 18–29 6.8% × 52M = 3.5M; 30–49 15% × 90M = 13.5M; 50–64 23% × 62M = 14.3M; 65+ 8.8% × 68M = 6.0M; total ≈ 37.3M = 13.7%. Income check: (18.0+13.0+10.1)/3 = 13.7. The middle third fell most (15→13) because it is the group most dependent on employer weight-management coverage, which is now retreating. The top third held up through cash longevity regimens and concierge care. The bottom third is roughly flat: Medicaid and ≈3.7M imported-product users offset losses. Of ≈32.4M off-now adults, an estimated ~5M stopped in this window because their coverage ended or an employer dropped the benefit, ~3M on medical advice (DEXA, GI symptoms), ~1.5M on principle, and the rest on cost or GI intolerance. About 2.9M current users have no obesity indication: ~1.6M on longevity/'metabolic health' regimens and ~1.3M on 'calm/focus' subscriptions. A further ~0.9M carry alcohol use disorder as their primary prescribing diagnosis. Pediatric: 0.45% of ~73M under-18s ≈ 330k, mostly 12–17 on semaglutide under specialist care; under-12 off-label use has nearly stopped in restriction states. About one US child in eight lives with a parent who is on the drug or cycling it. Adolescent bone-accrual interim data are underpowered and inconclusive.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: in Oct 2031 CMS renewed the Bridge successor rate at $199/month through Dec 2033 with no step-down. The $50 copay, the BMI/comorbidity criteria and the counselling visit with fall-risk screening are unchanged. Medicare pays ≈18% of fills ≈ 6.7M users (6.0M aged 65+ plus ≈0.7M disabled under-65), of whom ≈1.9M use the Bridge for obesity. 2032 Bridge spend: 1.9M × $199 × 12 ≈ $4.5B, up slightly from $4.3B because of volume at a flat price. Medicaid pays ≈9% of fills ≈ 3.4M users at $199: 3.4M × $199 × 12 ≈ $8.1B gross federal+state before supplemental rebates. Two states ended optional obesity coverage in 2031, citing the stalled price. Eleven states now explicitly cover incretins for AUD under their SUD benefit. The Indiana and Arkansas adherence waivers are unchanged.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 90+ semaglutide brands at $5–30/month, plus generic tirzepatide filings. China is the main API and finished-pen source for the gray trade. Canada: generic semaglutide at CAD 55–85/month. Brazil, Mexico and Turkey have generics. Generic oral semaglutide is sold in most markets outside the US and EU. EU generic semaglutide launched in several member states in 2031–32 after exclusivity lapsed.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Stalled and two-tier. Prices froze at the Dec 2029 levels: injectable semaglutide $199, tirzepatide $199–279, oral starting doses $149, higher oral doses $199, retatrutide $399 direct and $1,499 list. Two mechanisms held them there. First, the June 2031 patent settlements with generic filers set US generic semaglutide entry for 2033. Second, the 2031 renewal of the direct-portal deal carried no further cut, because the manufacturers cited Section 232 tariff costs and domestic-plant spending. Payer mix of ≈37.3M users: commercial 41% (15.3M), Medicare 18% (6.7M), Medicaid 9% (3.4M), cash/direct 22% (8.2M), imported/counterfeit 10% (3.7M) = 100%. Employer coverage for weight management fell from 63% to 49%. Many leavers kept coverage only for diabetes, cardiovascular, OSA, MASH and CKD codes. About 60% of commercial fills now carry one of those codes, against ~45% in 2030. Gating is less common among the employers that stayed (~55% of covering employers, down from ~70%) because the 2031 ADA ruling forced medical-pause exceptions that made gating costlier to run. The second tier is people with obesity alone and no qualifying code. They pay $199–279 a month cash (≈$2,400–3,350 a year), buy imports at $15–40, or go without. Non-obesity users (≈2.9M) are almost all cash: longevity regimens through concierge practices at $199–399 a month plus membership fees, and 'calm' subscriptions that in restriction states now need an in-person visit. The 503B exclusion and the 503A injunction stand.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, incl. 7.2 mg Wegovy dose)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: alcohol use disorder: guideline-endorsed second-line pharmacotherapy (ASAM/APA joint update and VA/DoD CPG, 2031) for semaglutide and tirzepatide, with no FDA label; Novo filed an AUD sNDA in Mar 2032, decision expected 2033
mainstream_offlabel_uses: longevity / 'metabolic health' low-dose regimens in people without obesity: mainstream in concierge and executive-health practices, ~1.6M users
'calm', 'focus' and 'craving freedom' subscriptions: shrinking under state restrictions and FTC consent orders, ~1.3M users
alcohol reduction below AUD threshold, often coded as mild AUD
smoking and vaping cessation (still off-label after the 2029 CRL; new trial enrolling)
gambling and compulsive-shopping craving reduction, still anecdotal
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care (sharply reduced in restriction states)
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. No new class reached market (next_gen_launch: none). Amycretin received a CRL in Aug 2031: its 72-week DEXA data showed lean-mass loss within range, but FDA asked for fracture-risk modelling in over-50s, and resubmission is planned for 2033. Survodutide's resubmission was accepted in 2031 with an extended goal date in Q1 2033. MariTide (filed Apr 2030) had its review extended in 2031 for bone and heart-rate data, with a decision expected 2033. Bimagrumab combinations remain in phase 3 and are not on the market. The AUD driver is realised as guideline endorsement plus an sNDA filing, not a label. The longevity driver is realised as mainstream off-label practice, with no indication. Incretin market ≈$114B in 2032, against ≈$118B in 2030: US net price flat, US volume down ~5%, ex-US branded revenue eroding further as EU generics arrive.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of voluntary discontinuation. Re-titration GI episodes are now common because drug holidays and cycling mean more people restart.
Elevated with rapid loss; stable incidence.
No causal confirmation; absolute risk low. Counterfeit-product cases still confound reporting.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL litigation ongoing, with no bellwether verdict yet.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Unchanged magnitude: ~30–40% of weight lost is lean mass in untrained users over 50. Resistance-training uptake has grown with the muscle ideal, but mainly among insured and affluent users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 2028 class label and 2029 joint guidance retained. No new statute.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal. Hip/vertebral HR ~1.3–1.4 in 65+ long-term users and ~1.2× in cycling postmenopausal women 50–64 hold in updated analyses. With ≈2.7M 65+ users on >2 years: 2.7M × 0.6% × 0.35 ≈ 5,700 excess hip fractures a year. DEXA waits have eased to 4–6 weeks in most regions as mobile capacity grows.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class labelling and the 2029 guidance retained. FDA bone endpoints are cited in the amycretin CRL. The DOJ civil matter against Novo is unresolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA warnings mention; no class determination.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association; AUD trial populations with high baseline risk showed no signal.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, 'the grey')
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal. The final retatrutide postmarketing SHAPS analysis (2031) matches the interim: ~11–13% of top-dose users cross a clinically meaningful threshold versus ~5% of comparators, still observational. Self-reported 'grey' is far more common than measured anhedonia. In the 2032 Pew survey, 29% of current users report it at some point.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Cited in the smoking-cessation CRL and in state restriction laws. FTC consent orders (2031) bar 'calm/focus' efficacy claims without RCT support. No label change.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Substantial regain within a year. The employer retreat has replaced gating terminations with benefit terminations as the main source of involuntary stops, and planned drug holidays add a new pattern of partial regain and re-titration.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly. The 2031 ADA ruling requires medical-pause exceptions in gated plans. The Seventh Circuit appeal on the Indiana waiver was argued in 2032 and is undecided.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D, calcium and protein signals persist in high-loss and older users. Longevity clinics screen routinely; imported-product users rarely do.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional guidance (2029) retained; no FDA action.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~7 years; adolescent exposure; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About ten years of follow-up, with no new long-horizon signal. Interim adolescent bone-accrual data (2032) are underpowered and inconclusive. Cycling still looks worse for bone than continuous use. Drug holidays are a new, unstudied form of short-cycle exposure.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements continue. Restriction-state laws set 18 as the minimum age for non-specialist prescribing.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination, substitution)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new mass-casualty cluster. Poison-centre calls have plateaued at the 2030 level while import volume grew ~20% (3.1M→3.7M users). Vial mg/unit confusion and injection-site infections continue.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alerts, seizures and pen-authentication guidance continue. Individuals are still not prosecuted; there is no new federal law.

safety_ledger.effect: Falls and frailty-related injury in older users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated fall-related ED visits in 65+ long-term users persist in claims data. The magnitude is still not separated from confounding, and no new signal has appeared.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Fall-risk screening remains in the Medicare counselling template.

food_and_beverage.state: Volume pressure eases slightly as current use dips and the 'fed' ideal returns appetite to fashion. Salty-snack volume is down ~1% a year against ~2–3% in 2029–30. Protein, dairy and 'bone-forward' lines still grow fastest. Heritage 'full portion' brands and premium meat gain with affluent under-35s chasing the muscled, well-fed look. Large packaged-food firms keep trimming SKUs and do not re-expand.

alcohol.state: Still contracting. The AUD guideline put incretins into addiction clinics, VA programmes and Medicaid SUD benefits, and heavy-drinker volumes keep falling. Spirits majors report a fourth and fifth year of US volume decline. A new wrinkle is drug-holiday weekends, which produce visible Friday–Saturday spikes in on-premise sales in suburbs with high uptake. Brewers market 'holiday' six-packs without saying the word.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat. Half portions and protein bowls remain standard. At the high end in New York, Los Angeles and Chicago, 'full appetite' tasting menus and steakhouse revivals court the aesthetic inversion and sell an unhurried, large meal as a status good. Value-volume buffet chains keep closing units, and the no-gram soul-food rooms in Atlanta and Houston keep growing.

apparel.state: Size churn continues, now with a cut shift: athletic and 'muscle fit' blocks with broader shoulders and fuller thighs replace slim fits in men's and women's premium lines. Fast fashion still sells to the thin-and-cheap mass market. Plus-size specialists are stable.

fitness.state: Growing. The muscle ideal and the bone guidance push the same way. Strength gyms, DEXA-plus-coaching chains and 'hypertrophy for women over 40' programmes are the fastest-growing segment. The growth skews affluent: strength coaching costs $150–400 a month, as much as the drug.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is retreating: 63% → 49%. With net price stuck at ≈$180–200 and no generic until 2033, the benefit never got cheaper. The 2031 ADA pause-exception ruling made gating costlier to administer, and bone-related claims added cost. Leavers keep diabetes, CV, OSA, MASH and CKD codes, and some add AUD under behavioural-health benefits, which drives audits of AUD coding. BMI-linked wellness surcharges remain. Pharmacy trend ~+4%.

pharma.state: Revenue is flat to slightly down (≈$114B): US price is frozen, US volume is down ~5%, and EU generics are arriving. Lilly still leads US volume. Novo leans on Medicare semaglutide and the AUD filing. Patent settlements protect the US through 2033. Bone-agent makers, DEXA suppliers and pen-authentication firms keep growing, and the concierge longevity channel is a profitable cash niche.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Thinness is cheap, so it no longer signals much. A $15 Indian pen or a $199 portal fill can buy it, and so it reads as neutral or faintly downmarket. The scarce look is muscle carried at a normal or above-normal weight, an evident appetite, and 'unmedicated vitality': color, energy, eating in public with pleasure. These are expensive to build without the drug and impossible to fake on it. The 'on it too long' look of thin arms and a forward stoop is now openly mocked in fashion media.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The gradient has inverted at the top. Affluent women 30–45 in Los Angeles and New York are the vanguard: they taper off or run low 'longevity' doses while paying for strength coaching, DEXA and nutritionists to build visible muscle. Middle-third workers who lost employer coverage are the most likely to have cycled off and regained, or to stretch a $199 cash pen. Bottom-third users on Medicaid or imports are now the visibly thin group. Thinness that once signalled money now often signals a cheap pen.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: The affluent table has turned performatively generous: whole fish, second helpings, 'I'm off this month'. Protein-first portions persist in offices and suburbs. Drug-holiday weekends make Saturday dinners bigger than weekday ones in households where someone is on the drug. Church potlucks and no-gram restaurants remain heritage spaces.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Profiles still state on/off, and many now say 'off by choice' or 'holiday weekends'. Among urban professionals under 40, 'unmedicated' has crossed over from backlash communities into a mainstream status marker. 'Strong' and 'eats' are the most-used appearance words in apps' 2032 trend reports.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has been re-valued as vitality. Fashion and wellness media, not only the backlash, now treat it as a sign of health and youth. The backlash coalition has partly won the aesthetic argument while losing control of it: luxury brands that never joined the Atlanta collectives or the Tulsa congregations sell their language back to them. The AUD guideline adds a counterweight, because for some people suppressing appetite is legitimately treatment.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Measured: ~11–13% of top-dose retatrutide users cross the SHAPS threshold versus ~5% of comparators (final postmarketing analysis, 2031, observational). Self-reported: in the 2032 Pew survey, 29% of current users (≈10.8M) say they have experienced 'the grey'. 38% (≈14M) take planned dose holidays or have deliberately lowered their dose, and 61% of those name mood, desire or creativity as a reason. AUD patients in addiction clinics describe the blunting as the point, which makes the complaint and the indication two readings of the same effect.
interior_life.framing: A side effect everyone knows about and manages. 'The grey' is ordinary speech, 'holiday weekend' is a verb, and dose-cutting before weddings, pitches and vacations is routine. In addiction medicine the same effect is framed as treatment ('quieting the reward loop'). The 'calm' marketing of 2029–30 has been rolled back by FTC consent orders and state laws, and the surviving brands sell 'clinician-guided dose management' instead.
interior_life.effect_on_work: With fewer employers paying, coverage leverage over workers has weakened, though diabetes-coded workers in gated plans still face adherence tracking with medical-pause exceptions after the ADA ruling. Sales, hospitality and creative workers openly schedule dose holidays around peak weeks. Some tech firms removed 'focus' subscriptions from lifestyle accounts after the FTC orders and California's law. Fleets still favour continuous use for OSA-coded drivers.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Fans and critics talk openly about 'grey albums'. Several musicians and comedians announce tapers as part of album and tour rollouts, and 'written off' (written unmedicated) has gone from a Nashville niche to a press-release cliché. Gaming and extreme-sport bookings among users remain elevated. Food writing has swung back to excess and pleasure.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Sex therapists treat dose as a routine variable. Couples coordinate holidays, and weekend-off households report more desire and more arguments alike. Fertility clinics advise pauses as standard. Mismatched holiday schedules are a sitcom premise.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Restriction laws passed with odd-coalition support: parents' groups, the backlash coalition and addiction-medicine clinicians in favour, telehealth firms and some patient groups against. The two-tier coverage split, with diabetes codes covered and obesity alone not, is now a kitchen-table issue in middle-income suburbs, used both for 'Medicare-for-weight' pitches and for 'stop paying for vanity' pitches. There is still no evidence of temperament effects on turnout.

state.regulatory_posture: Restrictive on marketing and minors, slow on approvals. FDA issued a CRL for amycretin and extended the MariTide and survodutide reviews over bone data. FTC consent orders (2031) with three telehealth brands bar 'calm/focus/anxiety' efficacy claims. California's Incretin Marketing and Minors Protection Act (2031) bans advertising for non-indicated uses, requires an in-person exam before a first prescription, sets 18 as the minimum age except under pediatric endocrinology or obesity-medicine specialists, and limits a first telehealth fill to 30 days. New York, Illinois and Washington enacted similar laws in 2032, covering ~25% of US adults in total. No federal statute. Import enforcement stays selective: no prosecution of individuals and no new importation law.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. The Medicare Bridge successor rate was renewed at $199 through 2033 with no step-down and the $50 copay. The federal direct-pricing portal holds the Dec 2029 prices. Medicaid coverage is state by state: two states dropped obesity coverage, and eleven cover AUD under SUD benefits. The VA added incretins to its AUD formulary in 2031.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The Indiana and Arkansas 1115 waivers are unchanged. Private gating has shrunk as employers exit, and the 2031 ADA ruling requires medical-pause exceptions in the plans that remain. Wellness rules allowing BMI-linked surcharges up to 30% of premium are unchanged. Payers now audit AUD diagnosis codes for 'weight-coverage laundering', and pharmacy weigh-in kiosks still serve Medicaid waiver states.
state.workforce_or_military: DOT sleep-apnea screening still makes tirzepatide a de facto requirement for some drivers. Fleets screen drivers over 55 with DEXA. Army accession policy on GLP-1 use is unchanged and contested. The VA is now the largest single AUD prescriber of incretins.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Indian and Chinese supply underpins ≈3.7M US import users. Section 232 tariffs remain, and manufacturers cited them in refusing further cuts in 2031. EU generic launches widen the transatlantic price gap and give US importation advocates a second reference point. India–US trade talks still treat mail-order pharma as a bargaining chip.

events.event: Federal judge in the Northern District of Illinois rules in Okafor v. Midwest Logistics Benefit Plan that ending GLP-1 coverage after a DEXA-advised pause violates the ADA, requiring medical-pause exceptions; within a year several large employers drop weight-management coverage entirely and keep only diabetes, cardiac and sleep-apnea codes

ASAM and the APA, followed by the VA/DoD guideline panel, endorse semaglutide and tirzepatide as second-line drugs for alcohol use disorder based on two phase 3 trials; the VA adds them to its AUD formulary and Novo files an sNDA in March 2032

Novo settles US patent litigation with five generic semaglutide filers, setting entry for 2033; in October HHS renews the direct-portal and Medicare price deal at the December 2029 levels of $199 for injectables and $149–199 for orals, with no further cut, after manufacturers cite tariff and plant costs

California enacts the Incretin Marketing and Minors Protection Act, which bans ads for uses without FDA approval, requires an in-person exam before a first prescription and sets 18 as the minimum age outside specialist care; FTC consent orders with Quiet and two rivals follow, and New York, Illinois and Washington pass similar laws in 2032

A national concierge-medicine network reports 400,000 members on low-dose 'healthspan' incretin protocols without obesity, as executive-health programs and longevity clinics make low-dose semaglutide a standard offering; analysts estimate 1.6M Americans on longevity regimens

Pew survey finds 38% of current GLP-1 users take planned dose holidays and 29% report 'the grey'; the same month New York agencies report bookings for muscular, 'fed' body types overtaking straight-size thin for the first time, and luxury houses run 'Appetite' campaigns

open_tensions: The two tiers have hardened. Diabetes, cardiac and sleep-apnea codes stay covered, while obesity alone is increasingly self-pay at $199–279 a month or an imported pen. Payers are auditing a growing use of AUD codes as a back door. The 2033 generic entry date is the next pressure point, and nobody knows whether employers will return when the price falls.

The muscle-and-appetite ideal is built on resistance training, DEXA and coaching that cost as much as the drug. The visibly thin are now disproportionately the bottom third on Medicaid or imports, so the drug's original class marker has flipped while still marking class.

Restriction laws covering a quarter of adults curb 'calm' marketing and teen telehealth starts, but they do not touch concierge longevity prescribing, which is in-person and cash. Off-label use by people without obesity has moved upmarket, not shrunk.

Reward blunting is a guideline-endorsed treatment in addiction medicine and a mainstream complaint everywhere else, managed with unstudied short-cycle drug holidays. The bone data already say cycling is worse, and no one has measured what weekend-off dosing does.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US; settlements now set entry for 2033.
Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
Oral starting doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) are still $149–150 a month cash through the federal direct-pricing portal (launched as TrumpRx) and manufacturer direct channels.

The Indiana and Arkansas Medicaid 1115 waivers still require ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered and quarterly verified weigh-ins, with two misses ending coverage for 12 months; the disability-rights litigation is still unresolved.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.

prose.headline: Thin Is Cheap Now: Why America's Rich Are Paying for Muscle, Appetite and the Right to Be 'Off'
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2032 slightly fewer Americans are on an incretin drug than two years ago, about 13.7 percent of adults against 14.6. The drugs did not fail, nothing frightening turned up, and no shortage interrupted supply. The prices simply stopped falling. In June 2031 Novo settled its patent fights with the generic makers and pushed American generic semaglutide to 2033. In the autumn the government renewed its price deal at the same numbers as before: $199 for an injectable on the federal portal, $149 for a starter pill, $199 for Medicare. Everyone had expected a new benefit to keep getting cheaper, and this one didn't.

Employers did the rest. A federal judge in Illinois ruled that a company plan could not cut off a worker's coverage for following her doctor's advice to pause for a bone scan. Gating had been the device that made the benefit affordable, and it suddenly needed exceptions, appeals and lawyers. Many companies stopped paying for weight loss entirely and kept coverage only for diabetes, heart disease and sleep apnea. Fewer than half of employers now cover the drugs for obesity. The middle-income worker with a high BMI and no diagnosis code is the person this story happens to. She pays $199 or $279 a month herself, or buys a pen from India, or stops and watches the weight return. More than four in ten people who have ever used these drugs have now stopped and restarted at least once.

The drug has found new work elsewhere. In 2031 the addiction-medicine societies and the VA endorsed semaglutide and tirzepatide for alcohol use disorder, and an FDA filing followed. Veterans' clinics prescribe it alongside naltrexone. Some state Medicaid programs pay for it under their substance-use benefits, and insurers have started auditing a suspicious rise in alcohol diagnoses among people whose weight coverage just ended. Meanwhile concierge practices in every affluent zip code sell low-dose 'healthspan' protocols to people who were never heavy, as a matter of course.

States pushed back where they could. California, then New York, Illinois and Washington, banned advertising for uses the FDA has not approved, required an in-person exam before a first prescription, and set eighteen as the age floor outside specialist care. The federal trade regulator forced the 'Quiet' and 'Even' subscription brands to drop their claims about calm and focus. The rules did reduce the number of teenagers getting the drug through telehealth. They did not touch the longevity clinic, where the doctor is in the room and the patient pays cash.

The cultural turn is the strangest part. Once thinness could be bought for $15 by mail, it stopped meaning much. In New York and Los Angeles the expensive look is now muscle carried at an ordinary weight, an appetite eaten in public, and a skin and energy fashion editors call 'unmedicated vitality'. That look takes coaches, scans and time. This spring the modeling agencies reported more bookings for muscular, 'fed' bodies than for straight-size thin ones. Luxury brands are selling the language of Atlanta's body-sovereignty collectives back to people who never joined them.

The flattening the drugs can bring is no longer a rumor or a product. It is a common complaint. Pew found that more than a third of users take planned breaks, usually weekends, weddings and pitch weeks, and nearly three in ten say they have felt 'the grey'. Bars notice the Fridays. Nobody has studied what weekend-off dosing does to bones that already dislike cycling.

From outside, the country looks steadier than it did in 2030. The bone wave has crested into routine scans, poison-centre calls have levelled off, and the snack aisle has stopped shrinking. What has changed is who gets what. The insured diabetic, the cash-paying longevity patient and the uninsured woman with a pen from Hyderabad now live under three different sets of rules for the same molecule.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Dana Reyes weighs herself at 6:10 because the habit outlasted the plan that required it. The kiosk at the Kroger in Grove City still blinks her name when she walks past.

The distribution company dropped weight coverage in January. Her supervisor, Phil, kept his, because Phil has a diabetes code. Dana's cash fill came Tuesday, tirzepatide through the portal, $279. She has started stretching each pen to ten days. Her telehealth doctor, a woman in Colorado she has never seen, told her not to, and Dana said okay.

At lunch the break room television runs an ad for a steakhouse: a woman with shoulders like a swimmer, tearing bread. Her nephew Mateo, sixteen, wants a lifting coach for Christmas. Two hundred a month.

Her sister texts from Phoenix: a photo of a box with Devanagari on the side, twenty-two dollars. *Real ones this time, I checked the lot.* Dana types *don't*, deletes it, and types *ok be careful*.

Saturday is Lucía's quinceañera, and Dana is skipping this week's dose so she can taste the tres leches and dance without the grey. Last time she did that, the nausea on restart took three days. She puts it on the calendar anyway: *restart Mon.*

After work she does the bodyweight squats from a free video. Her knees click. The instructor, unmedicated and glowing, says *eat like you mean it*.

At dinner she eats like she means it, half a plate, and stops when the quiet comes, and watches Mateo finish his second.
